## Tracks {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
Every track works on the same case and the same exercise. They differ in what stands in the foreground and in how much time they take. Each is an ordered route through pages already on this site, with a sidebar of its own and, at the end, the slide deck that the track uses. Choose one, and the site keeps your place in it.
:::

::: {.home-group}
One day
:::

:::: {.home-grid}

::: {.home-track .home-reveal data-slug="one-day-replication"}
### [One day – open science and replication](tracks/one-day-replication/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Four parts of ninety minutes, with a facilitator]{.home-meta}

The day in its original shape. You reproduce a recorded result, state the estimand behind the claim, finish its causal graph, explore a menu of defensible analyses and declare one before you run it.

<div class="home-units">

1. **Before the day** – Install R and an IDE, download the workspace, read the claim.
2. **Part 1 – Credibility and tools** – What a claim is for, why the field speaks of a crisis, and the toolchain.
3. **Part 2 – The claim and its estimand** – The paper in full, estimands and causal graphs.
4. **Part 3 – Reproduction and exploration** – The reproduction, then the specification menu.
5. **Part 4 – Multiverse and preregistration** – The class chart, and one analysis declared before it runs.
6. **After the day** – Where to go next in the companion curriculum.

</div>
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal data-slug="one-day-tools"}
### [One day – social data science tools](tracks/one-day-tools/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Four parts of ninety minutes, with a facilitator]{.home-meta}

The same case and exercise with the toolchain in the foreground: the language, the IDE, the document format, the packages, version control, and where finished work is archived.

<div class="home-units">

1. **Before the day** – Install R and an IDE, download the workspace, read the claim.
2. **Part 1 – Credibility and software** – The evidence on how often findings hold up, and why shared code mattered.
3. **Part 2 – The toolchain** – Each layer of the toolchain, then a first session in R.
4. **Part 3 – The claim and its reproduction** – The paper, its estimand and its graph, and the reproduction.
5. **Part 4 – Exploration, preregistration and archiving** – The menu, the declaration, and where the work is deposited.
6. **After the day** – Quarto, git and GitHub, and the rest of the curriculum.

</div>
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal data-slug="one-day-methods"}
### [One day – the statistical methods](tracks/one-day-methods/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Four parts of ninety minutes, with a facilitator]{.home-meta}

The same case and exercise with the statistics in the foreground: the causal-graph crash course in full, and the specification menu taken apart one decision at a time.

<div class="home-units">

1. **Before the day** – Install R and an IDE, read the claim, and fit one linear model.
2. **Part 1 – The case and the vocabulary** – The paper, the verdicts reached on it, and what 'replication' names.
3. **Part 2 – The claim and its estimand** – Estimands and the causal-graph crash course.
4. **Part 3 – Reproduction and the specification menu** – The reproduction, then the menu decision by decision.
5. **Part 4 – Multiverse and preregistration** – Reading the curve, and the analysis declared before it runs.
6. **After the day** – Every model on the menu, and the rest of the methods strand.

</div>
:::

## The case {.unnumbered}

::: {.home-intro}
A sociological paper of 2016 asked whether the economic crisis changed how citizens of the European Union frame the Union. One sentence of its abstract became the claim that this course works on.
:::

> "poor national economic performances significantly decrease positive EU-framing dimensions"

The case-study page tells the story in four parts: the original study, its data and the selections behind them; how SCORE and Multi100 set up their reanalyses; what the five reanalysts chose and how well their choices hold up; and how their results were standardised for comparison.

::: {.home-cta}
[Read the case study](case/index.qmd)
:::

::::

:::: {.home-rs .home-reveal}

::: {.home-r}
### Reproduction {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Two attempts to reproduce the published result from the original materials did not succeed.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Robustness {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Five analysts reanalysed the claim for Multi100. The partial correlations recorded for them run from −0.006 to −0.452.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Replication {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A replication on later Eurobarometer waves was judged not successful.
:::

## The exercise {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
Five tasks, in the order in which every track meets them.
:::

:::: {.home-reveal}

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 1</span>The setup check</summary>

Run the check script in the workspace, so that the rest of the work runs on a machine that is known to work.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 2</span>The panel, the estimand and the graph</summary>

Meet the country-year panel, write the estimand statement behind the claim, and finish the causal graph that goes with it.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 3</span>The reproduction</summary>

Reproduce t = −3.804, the value that Multi100 recorded for one of the five analysts, from the data behind it.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 4</span>The menu</summary>

Work through the decisions that lie between the data and a result, try alternatives one change at a time, and send one exploration to the class chart. The [decision map](exercise/estimand-dial.qmd) lays every decision out.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 5</span>Declaration and report</summary>

Declare one specification in a short preregistration, run it, report it, and see where it sits among the defensible alternatives on the [curve of the claim](results.qmd).

</details>

## The course {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

:::: {.home-reveal}

<details>
<summary>What the course teaches</summary>

This is a course with a workshop at its centre. The workshop runs as a single day of four 90-minute parts. The same case and the same exercise are also used in longer deliveries, over three days or across a semester, and a reader studying alone can work through them at their own pace.

The main aim of the course is to introduce technical skills for modern empirical data analysis: retrieving data from an online repository, working with code so that another person (or your future self) can reproduce your steps, fixing your analytical choices in a preregistration before you run the analysis, and writing a live report that combines code and text.

These skills are taught through an applied 'replication' exercise. Participants reproduce one of the reanalyses that made up the Multi100 project, whose results appeared in *Nature* [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. The reanalysis focuses on selected results from a *European Sociological Review* article [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic], testing the statistical robustness of a claim made by the original author (OA). You will:

1. **Reproduce a published analyst's result.** Run the submitted Multi100 analysis code on the original re-analysis data and find the exact coefficient it produced.
2. **See why five analysts got five different answers.** When you run the same code, you should get the same results; but there are different analysis options to choose from, and the five analysts each made different choices. Working through different analysis options involves engaging with and choosing between various statistical methods.
3. **State an _estimand_ and draw a causal graph.** Often, variation in methods and therefore results is driven by having an imprecise understanding of the *quantity* that the study is trying to estimate. That quantity is the *estimand*. Thinking about estimands is, first of all, a conceptual matter, as is thinking about the real-life relationships between the variables in your dataset. Causal graphs, or directed acyclic graphs or DAGs, are a useful way to visualise these relationships and decide what variables to adjust for.
4. **Preregister one specification.** Pick one defensible analysis from a menu of choices. Before you run it, fill in the preregistration block of your report, which is a shortened version of a real preregistration template: the claim you are testing, one option for each decision on the menu, and a sentence grounded in your causal graph on why you adjust for what you do.
5. **Run it and submit the result.** Your result appears as a point on a live chart, against the curve of the claim and, in a taught session, beside everyone else in the class.
6. **Read a specification curve.** Work out what the 864 specifications of the curve of the claim, taken together, can and cannot establish.

The exercise follows the design of Multi100 on a smaller scale, with many analysts testing the same claim, each stating their analytical choices, and results reported in a form that allows them to be compared.

</details>

<details id="four-blocks-ninety-minutes-each">
<summary>The workshop day</summary>

The workshop has this structure on the one-day course in open science and replication and in session 9 of the semester track. The tools-focused and methods-focused one-day formats keep four 90-minute parts but divide the material differently, and the three-day track teaches the first part on day 1 and runs the other three across the four sessions of day 2. Two breaks and a lunch separate the parts. When a delivery is scheduled, the callout near the top of this page gives its clock times.

| Part | Length | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Part 1 – Credibility and tools | 90 minutes | What social science is for and why people say it is in crisis; what open research proposes; the three Rs (reproducibility, robustness, replicability) and the evidence on each; and the computational toolchain that makes any of it checkable. |
| Break | | |
| Part 2 – The claim and its estimand | 90 minutes | The EU-frames paper in full, and why analysts who look like they disagree are often answering different questions. Estimands, causal graphs, and a DAG for the EU-frames case, which you finish yourself. |
| Lunch | | |
| Part 3 – Reproduction and exploration | 90 minutes | Reproducing the published result exactly, then working through the specification menu: what each analytical choice does, and what happens to the estimate when you change one. |
| Break | | |
| Part 4 – Multiverse and preregistration | 90 minutes | Reading the results from the class against the curve of the claim, on which the five reanalyses and the original study are marked; what a curve can and cannot establish; and settling on the one analysis you would defend, preregistered before you run it. |

</details>

<details id="two-routes-one-destination">
<summary>Running the analyses</summary>

The exercise is the same in every track, and it is done in R. Install R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.) once, before the day, then download a ready-made workspace – a single zip file holding the analysis code, the data and a report to fill in. There is nothing to configure and no account to create, so you open the folder and start working, and the workspace is yours to keep afterwards. The [Setup](setup.qmd) page walks you through the installation in plain steps.

The [Browser lab](exercise/browser-lab.qmd) page holds the same exercise and the same data on a version of R that runs inside a browser tab, with nothing installed. It is the page on which the facilitator demonstrates on a shared screen, the place to try R and the data before you have installed anything, and the fallback if a machine fails on the day. Anyone can use it, whether or not they are taking the course.

</details>

<details>
<summary>The companion curriculum</summary>

The [companion curriculum](companion/index.qmd) holds the teaching material of the course, arranged in three strands: computational tools, data management and sharing, and statistical methods. Every module keeps its own page and stands on its own, so you can read one for the skill it covers or take it in the place that a track gives it.

A single day has room for the exercise and very little else, which is why a one-day track points to the modules rather than working through them. The longer tracks are built out of them. The three-day track spends a day on the tools underneath the exercise and a day on the methods behind it, the semester track spreads the same modules across a term, and the self-study track puts them in an order that needs no facilitator at all.

</details>

## Chris Moreh {.unnumbered}

::: {.home-role}
Lecturer in Sociology, Newcastle University
:::

<!-- The biography is quoted from chrismoreh.com (source: D:/GitHub/chrismoreh-source/index.qmd), as CM asked on 2026-10-25. -->

A social scientist interested in the political sociology of migration, mobility, ethnicity and nationalism.

Hailing from Transylvania, trained in anthropology and sociology at [Eötvös Loránd University of Budapest](https://tatk.elte.hu/en/) and [Central European University](https://sociology.ceu.edu/), and with a PhD from [Northumbria University](https://www.northumbria.ac.uk/), I currently work as a Lecturer (Assistant Professor) in Sociology at [Newcastle University (UK)](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/gps/staff/profile/chrismoreh.html).

I approach social research as a comparative, interdisciplinary and multimethodological endeavour. My work has combined ethnographic observation, document analysis, survey methods and statistical modelling.

I'm enthusiastic about transparency and reproducibility in the social sciences, and my [pedagogical approach](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/mediav8/library/file-downloads/research-services/open-research/moreh.pdf) seeks to develop skills that facilitate open and credible research practices.

[chrismoreh.com](https://chrismoreh.com)
